question: What is the meaning of the use of standard ontologies in relation to certifications, standards, classifications and compliance, legal and regulatory information?
data_group: certifications, standards, classifications and compliance, legal and regulatory information
description: Standard ontologies provide a structured framework for capturing and representing information related to certifications, standards, classifications, and compliance, legal and regulatory information. They enable consistent and interoperable data modeling, facilitating the integration and exchange of information across different systems and domains. By leveraging standard ontologies, organizations can ensure that their data is aligned with industry standards and regulatory requirements, thereby enhancing compliance, traceability, and transparency in their operations. Additionally, standard ontologies support the automation of processes and decision-making, enabling more efficient and accurate management of certifications, standards, classifications, and compliance-related information. Overall, the use of standard ontologies in relation to certifications, standards, classifications, and compliance, legal and regulatory information, contributes to improved data quality, consistency, and interoperability, ultimately supporting better decision-making and regulatory compliance.

4.3.2. Competency questions 
Based on the results of the literature review and interviews, the 
following set of competency questions (CQs) are gathered. However, it 
should be mentioned that more CQs can be defined based on the iden­
tified IRs and specific use case at hand. Additionally, supplementary 
information S3 presents more CQs for some patterns to illustrate what 
the ontology can answer once it is populated with real data. 
CQ1. What is the serial number or unique identifier of the product? 
CQ2. What are the raw materials used in the product? 
CQ3. Where and when are the raw materials sourced from? 
CQ4. What is the composition of the materials used in the product? 
CQ5. What is the total carbon footprint of a product from raw ma­
terial extraction to consumer use? 
CQ6. What transport methods are used to deliver raw materials and 
components to the manufacturing side and what is the associated carbon 
footprint? 
CQ7. When was the product manufactured? 
CQ8. Which manufacturer manufactured the product and where is 
the manufacturing location? 
CQ9. What manufacturing processes were used? 
CQ10. Which suppliers provide materials or components for a given 
product, and where are these suppliers located? 
CQ11. What are the transport methods used to deliver the product 
and what is the associated carbon footprint? 
CQ12. What are the intended functionality and performance criteria 
for the product? 
CQ13. What certifications has the product obtained (for example, 
eco-labels, safety certifications)? 
CQ14. What are the assembly, disassembly, maintenance and care 
instructions for the product? 
CQ15. Who were the designers, engineers, and others involved in the 
creation of the product? 
4.3.3. Key notions and patterns identification 
Key notions are derived from the results of literature review and 
interviews, which are also stated in the use case description and com­
petency questions. They are the fundamental concepts that will be used 
in the modeling work (Shimizu et al., 2023). The core principle is that 
each identified key notion will evolve into a module (Shimizu et al., 
2023). 
Following the identification of key notions, they were aligned with 
existing core ontologies to ensure interoperability and wider coverage of 
the scope of the ontology. Additionally, a suitable or adaptable pattern is 
selected to be used as a template to model the first draft of the corre­
sponding module (Shimizu et al., 2023). We used syntactic and semantic 
conditions for pattern selection (Aranguren et al., 2008). For syntactic 
matching, we focused on reading pattern documentations and exam­
ining example competency questions provided in the documentation. 
We also targeted class names and annotations found in label or comment 
for exact matches and regular expression (pattern) matches. For 
matching with semantic condition, we examined the pattern's logical 
structure and applied it to our classes that matched a specific class 
expression. This involves looking beyond the textual content (syntactic 
aspects) of the ontology elements and focusing on the semantic re­
lationships and structures defined in the pattern's logical framework. It 
is worth mentioning that it may be necessary to use multiple patterns to 
fully represent a single key notion (Shimizu et al., 2023).
